domain: Religious Studies / Japanese History / Ontology of Practice
topic_summary: Analysis of shinbutsu-shugo (Shinto-Buddhist syncretism) in pre-Meiji Japan, examining whether centuries of simultaneous practice constituted a single fused ontological commitment or a domain-partitioned coexistence. The kernel contest centers on whether the syncretic reading (one unified cosmology) and the partition reading (separate jurisdictions for life-cycle vs death rituals) represent genuinely different interpretations of the same commitment or expose an incoherent bundle that was never truly unified.

key_entities: Kami (Shinto deities, nature spirits, ancestral presences)
Honji-suijaku theory (doctrinal framework: kami as local manifestations of universal buddhas)
Meiji government (1868+ state apparatus enforcing shinbutsu-bunri separation)
Local practitioners (village-level ritual participants across centuries)
key_tensions: Doctrinal fusion (honji-suijaku hierarchical subsumption) vs practical coexistence (parallel ritual systems)
Elite interpretive authority (Buddhist clergy theorizing kami-buddha identity) vs folk practice (pragmatic multi-ontology navigation)
key_mechanisms: Honji-suijaku mapping (systematic identification of kami with specific buddhas/bodhisattvas)
Ritual domain allocation (birth/marriage/harvest to Shinto; death/afterlife to Buddhism)
Shinbutsu-bunri enforcement (Meiji state forcibly separating shrines from temples, 1868-1874)
key_absences: Practitioner testimony on ontological coherence (historical record dominated by elite doctrinal texts)
Pre-Buddhist Shinto baseline (no clear archaeological/textual record of 'pure' Shinto before 6th century contact)

commitment_system_recognition.kernel_description: The ontological status of kami-buddha relationship: whether simultaneous veneration constitutes unified cosmology or domain-partitioned coexistence
commitment_system_recognition.authority_description: Buddhist clergy held interpretive authority via honji-suijaku doctrine; Meiji state later claimed authority to define 'authentic' Shinto via separation edicts; folk practice operated without explicit interpretive claims

readings.commitment: Kami and buddhas are ontologically unified: kami are local manifestations (suijaku) of universal buddha-nature (honji)
readings.authority_grounding: Buddhist doctrinal hierarchy via honji-suijaku theory; Tendai/Shingon scholastic frameworks
readings.expected_structural_delta: Single cosmological constraint; hierarchy with buddhas as ontological ground; kami subordinated but not eliminated; beneficiary: Buddhist institutional authority

readings.commitment: Kami and buddhas govern separate jurisdictional domains: kami for this-worldly life-cycle events, buddhas for death and afterlife
readings.authority_grounding: Folk practice patterns; ritual specialization without doctrinal unification claim
readings.expected_structural_delta: Two parallel constraints with non-overlapping scope; no hierarchy claim; coexistence without subsumption; beneficiary: local ritual autonomy

readings.commitment: No unified ontology existed: practitioners navigated contradictory frameworks opportunistically without resolving incompatibility
readings.authority_grounding: Anthropological/historical analysis of practice-doctrine gap; post-Meiji retrospective interpretation
readings.expected_structural_delta: Constraint bundle without coherence; multiple incompatible extractiveness structures operating simultaneously; victim: ontological consistency; beneficiary: ritual flexibility

axiom_contradictions.basis: Fusion reading requires that a single coherent cosmology unified kami-buddha identity; incoherence reading requires that no such unification occurred and practitioners held contradictory commitments simultaneously. No framework can hold both: either the ontology was unified or it was not.

axes.structural_delta: Whether simultaneous kami-buddha veneration constituted unified cosmology, domain partition, or incoherent bundle
axes.primary_observable: Honji-suijaku doctrinal texts vs ritual practice patterns vs practitioner testimony (where available); Meiji separation enforcement as stress test
axes.selection_reason: Core contested kernel; three distinct readings with different ontological commitments and structural deltas

axes.structural_delta: State apparatus forcibly separating shrine-temple complexes and redefining 'authentic' Shinto as non-Buddhist
axes.primary_observable: Separation edicts (1868-1874); jingu-ji destruction/conversion rates; clergy reclassification records
axes.selection_reason: Independent structural delta (state coercion mechanism); downstream of kernel; tests kernel coherence via forced choice

omegas.description: Historical record dominated by elite doctrinal texts and Meiji-era retrospective accounts. Direct practitioner testimony on ontological coherence largely absent. Cannot definitively adjudicate between readings without access to pre-Meiji folk ontological commitments.
omegas.source: Absence Inventory (§1.1) + F34 epistemic trespass boundary

omegas.description: No clear archaeological or textual record of 'pure' Shinto before 6th-century Buddhist contact. Syncretic fusion reading may be anachronistic projection; domain partition reading may assume a pre-existing Shinto structure that never existed as discrete system.

Meiji separation edicts created the category 'Shinto' as distinct from Buddhism. Modern scholarship may inherit this constructed boundary, making it difficult to assess whether pre-Meiji practitioners experienced ontological tension or seamless integration.
omegas.source: Dark Matter Probe 3 (Beneficiary Scan) + historical contingency of separation

omegas.description: Relationship between syncretic_fusion and domain_partition readings unclear: are they mutually exclusive (one forecloses the other) or complementary (elite doctrine vs folk practice, both true simultaneously)? Edge type affects whether this is licensed plurality or genuine contest.

fracture_scan.notes: F34 detected: Model lacks direct access to pre-Meiji Japanese religious phenomenology and practitioner testimony. Readings are reconstructions from elite texts and anthropological inference. Generated omega_practitioner_testimony_gap and omega_pre_buddhist_baseline to bound this limitation. Pragmatic_incoherence_reading is itself a modern scholarly interpretation that may not reflect historical experience.
